name: Chinchorro red mummy pigment

card.summary: The red ochre coating and black manganese paste that the Chinchorro of northern Chile used to finish preserved bodies, an ancient example of colour and modelling applied to a face and body to present a lasting appearance.
card.aka: Chinchorro red mummies, red ochre mummification
card.note: Historical and archaeological topic; pigments were funerary, not a product for living skin.

quick.overview:
The Chinchorro people of the Pacific coast of northern Chile and southern Peru began artificially preserving their dead by about 5050 BCE. In the red style, dated roughly 2570 to 2090 BCE, bodies were coated with red ochre, fitted with human-hair wigs and given modelled faces.
For the wiki it is an early record of cosmetic craft: colour, wigs and sculpted features used to give the dead a deliberate, lasting look. Archaeologists generally read it as part of an ancestor cult rather than as everyday beauty practice.
quick.how: Archaeological descriptions say the body was opened to remove organs, dried with hot coals and ashes, stiffened with thin wooden poles and packed with feathers, soil and camelid fibre. The head was refitted, a wig held with black manganese paste, and the body covered in red ochre while the face was typically left black.
quick.risks: There is no living-use practice to caution against; the topic is archaeological. Mineral pigments such as manganese compounds are not documented as skincare products.

lead: Chinchorro red mummies are bodies of the Chinchorro culture of northern Chile and southern Peru that were reconstructed and finished with red ochre, dated to about 2570 to 2090 BCE. Sites include Arica, Camarones, Punta Pichalo, Bajo Molle and Patillos.[1]

The finish combined colour and styling. The body was covered with red ochre, the face was generally left black, and a human-hair wig, which could reach about 60 cm, was fixed with black manganese paste over a modelled face.[1] Earlier black mummies (about 5000 to 2800 BCE) were finished with a manganese dioxide paint over clay modelling.[1]
Researchers consider the Chinchorro among the earliest cultures to practise deliberate artificial mummification, which gets brief coverage in reviews of embalming history.[2]

angle.goal: Historical context for pigment and appearance
chain: Mineral pigments (red ochre, manganese) applied to a reconstructed body
Wig, modelled face and colour create a deliberate presentation
Ancestors displayed and kept among the living
angle.text: This is a historical example of colour, wigs and facial modelling used to shape how a person looked, in a funerary setting. It shows long-standing human use of mineral pigment for appearance but is not a method for living people.

paras: In the red style the body was not fully disassembled as in the black style. Incisions at shoulders and groin allowed organs and some muscle to be removed, the head was detached to take out the brain, and cavities were dried with coals and ashes. Thin wooden poles went under the skin of arms, legs and spine, and cavities and head were packed with seabird feathers, soil and camelid fibre, with incisions sewn using human hair or reed fibre.[1]
The head was reattached with a wig of human hair, held by black manganese paste, and the features were modelled. The body was coated with red ochre, the face generally left black.[1]

Proposals include helping the soul survive and keeping the bodies from frightening the living. The more widely accepted view is an ancestor cult: bodies travelled with groups, held places of honour in rituals, and were not permanently buried until some time after death.[1]

Pre-Columbian South American mummies, mainly from the Chiribaya and Chinchorro cultures, have been the subject of palaeopathology studies of disease and age; a meta-analysis found 61 Pubmed-listed studies (1977 to 2005) covering over 6,400 mummified individuals.[3] Embalming-history reviews cite the Chinchorro alongside Egyptian practice as early preservation.[2]
No studies found on the pigment as a cosmetic or on living skin. The research on Chinchorro mummies is archaeological and palaeopathological.[3]

timeline.event: Artificial mummification begins among the Chinchorro.[1]
